extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry) / learners of scheme theory
extracted.subtask_description: Define and characterize many commonly used classes of morphisms of schemes (open embeddings, affine, quasicompact, quasiseparated, finite, integral, etc.), and state the key lemmas/theorems one uses to check or deduce these properties. Includes exercises, examples, and proof sketches used in a graduate course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local on the target
rubrics_metrics.description: A class of morphisms is local on the target: if π : X → Y is in the class, then for any open V ⊂ Y the restricted morphism π^{-1}(V) → V is in the class; conversely, if Y has an open cover {V_i} and each restricted morphism π^{-1}(V_i) → V_i is in the class, then π is in the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of three properties expected of any “reasonable” type of morphism; it allows checking the property on an open (often affine) cover of the target (see §7.0.2 and 7.1.1). Use the Affine Communication Lemma to reduce to affine checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed under composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y and ρ : Y → Z are both in the class, then their composition ρ ∘ π : X → Z is also in the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the three characteristic properties of reasonable morphism classes; used repeatedly to build new examples from known ones (see §7.1.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed under base change (stable under pullback)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a morphism π : X → Y is in the class, then for any Z → Y the base change X ×_Y Z → Z is also in the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third characteristic property of reasonable morphism classes; essential for geometric behavior and for checking properties fiberwise (see §7.1.1 and exercises such as 7.1.B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open embedding (open immersion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An open embedding (open immersion) of schemes is a morphism π : (X, O_X) → (Y, O_Y) that factors as an isomorphism followed by the inclusion of an open subset (i.e., π factors as X ≃ (U, O_Y|_U) ↪ Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequences: isomorphisms are open embeddings; one often says X is an open subscheme of Y. Exercises 7.1.A and 7.1.B ask to verify properties (i) and (ii), and property (iii) (stability under base change) is treated in 7.1.B as an important exercise. Note: the notion is not local on the source (Exercise 7.1.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local on the source
rubrics_metrics.description: A property P of morphisms is local on the source if to check π : X → Y has P it suffices to check on an open cover {U_i} of X (i.e., each restriction π|_{U_i} has P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can similarly define affine-local on the source by checking on affine covers of X. This notion is distinct from 'local on the target' and matters for how to verify properties (see §7.1.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local on the source/target
rubrics_metrics.description: Affined-local means the property can be checked on any affine cover of the source (resp. target): it suffices that the restriction to each affine open satisfies the condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes 'affine-local' to indicate the simplicity of affine checks; several properties (affineness, quasicompactness, quasiseparatedness, finiteness) are affinelocal on the target (see 7.3.4, 7.3.C, 7.3.G). Use the Affine Communication Lemma 5.3.2 to pass between local and global.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompact morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasicompact if for every open affine U ⊂ Y the preimage π^{-1}(U) is quasicompact (equivalently the preimage of any quasi-compact open is quasi-compact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasicompactness is useful because finite covers and inductive arguments become available. Many reasonable schemes are quasicompact (e.g., schemes from Noetherian sources). See Exercises 7.3.A–C for basic permanence properties and locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparated morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasiseparated if for every affine open U ⊂ Y the scheme π^{-1}(U) is quasiseparated (i.e., the intersection of two affines is covered by finitely many affines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasiseparatedness is often paired with quasicompactness (qcqs). The acronym qcqs is used widely; many natural morphisms (affine, from Noetherian schemes, separated) are quasiseparated. See 7.3.1 and Exercises 7.3.B and 7.3.C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is affine if for every affine open set U ⊂ Y, the preimage π^{-1}(U) (interpreted as an open subscheme of X) is an affine scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affine morphisms are quasicompact and quasiseparated (Exercise 7.3.D). Affineness is affine-local on the target (Proposition 7.3.4): if Y has an affine cover on which π is affine, then π is affine. The proof uses the Qcqs Lemma and the Affine Communication Lemma; see 7.3.7 for the proof sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qcqs Lemma (Γ(X,O_X)_s ≃ Γ(X_s,O_X))
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is quasicompact and quasiseparated and s ∈ Γ(X, O_X), then the natural map Γ(X, O_X)_s → Γ(X_s, O_X) is an isomorphism (where X_s is the locus where s doesn’t vanish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is the technical datum behind many gluing/affineness arguments (used in the proof of Proposition 7.3.4). The proof reduces to checking exactness on finite affine covers and then localizing; the qcqs hypotheses guarantee finite products and commuting localization (see §7.3.5–7.3.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is finite if for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y, the preimage π^{-1}(Spec B) is Spec A where A is a B-algebra that is a finitely generated B-module (i.e., A is a finite B-algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By definition finite morphisms are affine. Warning: 'finite' (finitely generated as a module) is stronger than 'finitely generated as an algebra'. Finiteness is affine-local on the target (Exercise 7.3.G). Typical properties: finite morphisms have finite fibers and are closed maps (Exercises 7.3.K and 7.3.M). Examples: branched covers given by k[t] over k[u] when u = p(t); closed embeddings Spec A/I → Spec A; normalizations; morphisms to Spec k that are finite give finite discrete sets of points with finite residue extensions (Exercise 7.3.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral morphism / integral homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring homomorphism φ : B → A is integral if every element of A satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in φ(B). A morphism of schemes is integral if it is affine and the corresponding ring maps are integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite implies integral (Corollary 7.2.2), but integral need not imply finite. Geometric translation: if L/K is a field extension then Spec L → Spec K is integral iff L/K is algebraic. The Lying Over and Going-Up theorems are fundamental results about integral extensions (see 7.2.5–7.2.6 and 7.2.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite implies integral (finite ⇒ integral)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finite B-algebra (i.e., A is a finitely generated B-module), then the inclusion B → A is an integral homomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as Corollary 7.2.2 and follows because elements of a finite B-module generate a finite subalgebra closed under multiplication, giving an integral equation via the adjugate/determinant trick (Lemma 7.2.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms have finite fibers
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is finite then for each point y ∈ Y the fiber π^{-1}(y) is a finite set (as a topological set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 7.3.K asks to prove this by reducing to the affine case and then to the case of a finite algebra over a field. The proof uses localization/modding out by primes to focus on fibers and the preservation of finiteness under these operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: finite fibers do not imply finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism can have finite fibers yet fail to be finite (e.g., the open embedding A^2 − {(0,0)} → A^2 has finite fibers but is not affine and hence not finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 7.3.9 and Exercise 7.3.L for examples illustrating that having finite fibers is not sufficient to conclude finiteness; one also needs algebraic/module-finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-locality of finiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Finiteness of a morphism is affine-local on the target: π : X → Y is finite iff Y has an affine cover {Spec A_i} such that each π^{-1}(Spec A_i) is the spectrum of a finite A_i-algebra (Exercise 7.3.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets one check finiteness by checking finite algebra conditions on an affine cover of the target. Combine with standard localization and quotient permanence properties of integrality (Exercises 7.2.B and 7.2.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying Over Theorem (integral extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : B → A is an integral extension then for every prime ideal q ⊂ B there exists a prime ideal p ⊂ A such that p ∩ B = q. Equivalently, Spec A → Spec B is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Theorem 7.2.5 and has a geometric interpretation: above every downstairs prime there exists an upstairs prime. The proof uses localization at q and maximal ideals in A and reduces to Exercise 7.2.E (field case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Going-Up Theorem (integral extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : B → A is integral and q_1 ⊂ q_2 ⊂ ... ⊂ q_n is a chain of primes of B and p_1 ⊂ ... ⊂ p_m (m < n) is a chain of primes of A lying over q_1 ⊂ ... ⊂ q_m, then the chain can be extended to a chain p_1 ⊂ ... ⊂ p_n of primes of A with p_i ∩ B = q_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulated as Exercise 7.2.F (the Going-Up Theorem). The usual strategy is to reduce to basic cases (m=1, n=2, etc.) and apply Lying Over and integrality arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakayama's Lemma (several useful versions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various equivalent forms: (1) If A is a ring, I ⊂ A an ideal, and M a finitely generated A-module with M = IM, then there exists a ∈ A with a ≡ 1 (mod I) and aM = 0. (2) If I is contained in all maximal ideals and M finitely generated with M = IM, then M = 0. (3) If (A, m) local and f_1,...,f_n generate M/mM then they generate M (lifting generators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use the adjugate/determinant trick from Lemma 7.2.1; Nakayama is used repeatedly (Exercises 7.2.7–7.2.I) and has geometric interpretations (Exercise 13.7.E). Important for statements about generating sets and behavior modulo maximal ideals.
